phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: Watch where it hunts on damp lawns — what is it pulling up?
It builds a mud-lined nest in a tree fork

blurb: A lawn-hunting thrush whose carolling opens the dawn chorus.
deeper: Robins find worms by sight, not sound — the head-tilt aims one eye at the soil. In autumn they switch to fruit and become major seed carriers.

phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: It follows anything that disturbs soil
Look for dense evergreen cover nearby

blurb: Orange-breasted and bold, it sings even under winter streetlights.
deeper: Both sexes hold winter territories and sing to defend them, which is why the robin is one of the few birds heard all year.

phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: Chicks need insects — find what the parents are catching
Colonies roost in dense hedges and creepers

blurb: The chattering companion of human settlement for ten thousand years.
deeper: Chicks are raised almost entirely on insects, so a street without bugs is a street without sparrows — their decline tracks the loss of urban invertebrates.

phenotypes.name: Blue-bar (wild type)
phenotypes.hint: Grey with two black wing bars

phenotypes.name: Checker
phenotypes.hint: Wings chequered dark

phenotypes.name: Pied
phenotypes.hint: Splashed with white

phenotypes.name: Ash-red
phenotypes.hint: Rusty brown replaces the grey

links.hint: Something hunts these flocks from the tallest ledges
Find the weedy seeds it gleans

blurb: A cliff-nester that mistook our buildings for sea cliffs.
deeper: Town flocks carry many colour morphs because they descend from domestic breeds. They are the staple that lets falcons live downtown.

links.hint: Document the flocks it hunts
Open sky over water gives it room to stoop

acoustic.sounds: Harsh, scolding kak-kak-kak near the nest

blurb: The fastest animal alive, now nesting on bridges and towers.
deeper: Recovered from near-extinction after DDT was banned. Nest ledges are reused for decades, which is exactly why their locations are kept obscured.

phenotypes.name: Dark morph
phenotypes.hint: Chocolate-brown body, still with the brick-red tail

phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: Find the tall perching tree it watches from
Document its prey — squirrels and voles
Log it over the rough grass that feeds its prey

blurb: The broad-winged watcher of roadsides and field edges.
deeper: A hawk on a pole is a sign of a working food web below: rough grass, the voles within it, and a tall perch to watch from.

links.hint: Small mammals are almost its entire diet
Log it over tussocky, unmown grass

acoustic.sounds: A long, rasping shriek — never a hoot

blurb: A pale ghost quartering rough grassland at dusk.
deeper: Its heart-shaped face is a sound dish; it can strike a vole in total darkness. One pair needs thousands of small mammals a year — and the tussocky grass that grows them.

links.hint: It needs big trees with old stick nests
Rabbits, squirrels and skunks are all on the menu

acoustic.sounds: Deep, stuttering hoots: hoo, hoo-hoo, hoo, hoo

blurb: The deep-voiced night hunter of woods and suburbs.
deeper: It nests in midwinter, taking over old hawk and crow nests, so its hooting duets peak when the trees are bare.

phenotypes.name: Eclipse drake
phenotypes.hint: Late-summer male in hen-like plumage with a yellow bill

phenotypes.name: Breeding drake
phenotypes.hint: Glossy green head and curled tail feathers

links.hint: Hens hide nests in waterside vegetation
It dabbles for seeds and shoots

blurb: The familiar dabbling duck, ancestor of most farmyard ducks.
deeper: In late summer drakes moult into a drab 'eclipse' plumage and briefly cannot fly — look for the tell-tale yellow bill.

links.hint: Find the flying insects it is hawking
It needs wet mud nearby to build its nest cup

acoustic.sounds: Cheerful twittering ending in a dry rattle

blurb: A fork-tailed long-distance migrant that feeds entirely on the wing.
deeper: Each bird crosses continents twice a year. Its arrival date is one of the oldest phenology records humans keep.

links.hint: Find the caterpillars it feeds its brood
It nests in tree holes

blurb: A bold, black-capped acrobat of woods and feeders.
deeper: It times its brood to the brief peak of oak caterpillars. As springs warm, birds and caterpillars are drifting out of step.

links.hint: It excavates nests in soft, rotting wood
In summer it gleans insects from bark and leaves

acoustic.sounds: Whistled fee-bee, and a buzzy chick-a-dee-dee-dee

blurb: A tiny, curious bird that stays through the hardest winters.
deeper: Each autumn it grows new neurons to remember thousands of seed caches. More 'dee' notes in its call means a more dangerous predator.

phenotypes.name: Yellow morph
phenotypes.hint: A golden bird where red should be — exceptionally rare

phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: It nests low in dense shrubs and vines
Seeds and berries colour its feathers

acoustic.sounds: Loud slurred whistles: cheer, cheer, birdie-birdie

blurb: The crested red songster of hedges and backyards.
deeper: The male's red comes from pigments in its food. A rare mutation blocks the conversion, producing a yellow cardinal — roughly one in a million.

phenotypes.name: Breeding plumage
phenotypes.hint: Brilliant yellow with a black cap

phenotypes.name: Winter plumage
phenotypes.hint: Soft olive-brown with buffy wing bars

links.hint: It feeds on seedheads — leave them standing
Log it in weedy, unmown ground

blurb: A late-nesting finch that waits for thistledown.
deeper: One of very few songbirds that moults twice a year, so the same bird is lemon-yellow in July and olive-drab in January.

links.hint: Find the tubular flowers it visits

blurb: A three-gram migrant that crosses the Gulf of Mexico non-stop.
deeper: Red tubular flowers evolved around this bird's bill. Its spring arrival tracks the northward bloom of its nectar plants.

phenotypes.name: Breeding plumage
phenotypes.hint: Glossy purple-green with a yellow bill

phenotypes.name: Winter plumage
phenotypes.hint: Covered in white spots, dark bill

links.hint: It probes lawns for grubs
Murmurations are a defence — against what?

acoustic.sounds: Wheezes, clicks, rattles and stolen phrases

blurb: A glossy mimic famous for its swirling evening murmurations.
deeper: About a hundred birds released in New York in 1890 became some two hundred million, out-competing native hole-nesters across a continent.

phenotypes.name: Leucistic
phenotypes.hint: Pale or patchy white plumage from a rare pigment mutation

links.hint: Watch it listen and stab on wet lawns
Find the winter berries it carries away

acoustic.sounds: Slow, mellow fluting that ends in a squeaky flourish

blurb: The fluting evening voice of gardens.
deeper: Blackbirds strip ivy and rowan berries in winter and deposit the seeds far away — a quiet forester of hedgerows.

links.hint: It nests in tree hollows — and fights for them
It follows grazing animals and mowers for flushed insects

acoustic.sounds: Gurgles, squawks and whistles in rapid mix

blurb: A confident, yellow-masked starling of towns and fields.
deeper: Beloved at home, but among the world's most damaging invasive birds elsewhere, evicting native parrots from nest hollows.

links.hint: Find the big trees where it roosts communally
Another bird is hiding eggs in its nest — listen for it

blurb: The grey-collared crow that lives wherever people do.
deeper: It is found almost nowhere without humans. Its nests are the chosen nursery of the Asian koel.

links.hint: Whose nest raises its chicks?
Find the fruiting fig it feeds in

blurb: A hidden cuckoo whose rising call announces the hot season.
deeper: A brood parasite: the female slips her egg into a crow's nest. As a fig-eater she is also a key planter of banyans.

phenotypes.name: Lutino
phenotypes.hint: All-yellow escapee morph

phenotypes.name: Blue morph
phenotypes.hint: Sky-blue aviary mutation

links.hint: It nests in old tree hollows
Find the fruiting tree the flock raids

blurb: A lime-green parrot at home from Sahel scrub to London parks.
deeper: Escaped cage birds now breed across Europe, competing with bats and woodpeckers for tree hollows.

links.hint: It listens for grubs under turf
Find its nest tree

blurb: A black-and-white songster with a flute-like dawn carol.
deeper: Family groups hold the same territory for years and recognise individual human faces.

links.hint: Find the flowering tree the flock is working

blurb: A brush-tongued parrot that chases the eucalypt bloom.
deeper: Its tongue ends in a brush for mopping nectar and pollen, making it a major pollinator of gum trees.

links.hint: Find what it sallies out to catch
It often hunts from perches over water

blurb: A bold yellow flycatcher that shouts its own name.
deeper: It fishes like a kingfisher, hawks insects like a flycatcher and eats fruit like a thrush — a generalist thriving in cities.

links.hint: Check the leaf undersides for a striped specialist
Find who visits its flowers

blurb: A milky-sapped meadow plant with globes of fragrant pink flowers.
deeper: Its toxins defend it from almost everything except a few specialists that turn the poison into their own armour.

links.hint: Search the leaves for banded caterpillars
Carpenter bees are its main pollinators — who is visiting?

blurb: A waxy-flowered giant milkweed of waysides and wasteland.
deeper: Often dismissed as a weed, it is the nursery of tiger butterflies; its floss once stuffed pillows.

links.hint: Find an early pollinator feeding on it

blurb: The sun-yellow first meal of spring for hungry pollinators.
deeper: Each 'flower' is around a hundred florets. Its deep taproot mines calcium and loosens compacted soil.

phenotypes.name: Four-leaf
phenotypes.hint: A lucky mutation — roughly 1 in 5,000 leaves

links.hint: Its flowers are built for bees — find one at work

blurb: A creeping lawn legume that feeds bees and soil alike.
deeper: Bacteria in its root nodules pull nitrogen from the air, fertilising the grass around it for free.

links.hint: Find a pollinator on the cone
Who eats the seedheads in autumn?

blurb: A prairie daisy with a bristling orange cone.
deeper: It feeds in two seasons: nectar for butterflies in summer, then oily seeds for finches if the heads are left standing.

links.hint: Find a long-tongued visitor

blurb: Shaggy lavender pom-poms smelling of oregano.
deeper: Its tubular florets fit long tongues: bumblebees, hawk-moths and hummingbirds.

links.hint: Look for leaves folded into tents
Who patrols it for aphids?

blurb: The stinging herb that is a butterfly nursery in disguise.
deeper: A nettle patch can raise several butterfly species and shelter the aphids that feed spring ladybirds.

links.hint: Which birds hide or nest in the stand?
Log it in standing water or a marsh

blurb: The brown-sausage reed of marsh edges.
deeper: Its stands filter run-off and hide nests; a single spike releases some two hundred thousand seeds.

links.hint: Its roots depend on woodland fungi — find any nearby
Log it beneath a closed canopy

blurb: A three-petalled spring ephemeral of old woodland.
deeper: It takes seven years or more to flower and its seeds are planted by ants. Picked and poached, colonies rarely recover.

links.hint: No fungus, no orchid — log a fungus in the same ground
It needs unfertilised, lightly-mown grassland

blurb: An orchid whose flower impersonates a female bee.
deeper: The disguise evolved to lure male bees into mating with it. Its dust-like seed cannot germinate without a partner fungus.

links.hint: Record which woodland flowers it is displacing

blurb: A garlic-scented hedgerow herb — and a woodland invader abroad.
deeper: Its roots leak chemicals that poison the soil fungi native wildflowers and tree seedlings depend on.

links.hint: Record the bankside plants at its edge

blurb: Bamboo-like canes forming dense thickets along rivers and rail lines.
deeper: A fingernail of root regrows a whole stand. Never cut and dump it — report it to the land manager.

links.hint: Who drinks from its late flowers?
Who eats or hides in it?

blurb: An evergreen climber: wildlife larder at home, smothering carpet abroad.
deeper: In Europe its autumn flowers are the last big nectar source of the year. In North American forests it forms 'ivy deserts' and topples trees.

links.hint: Which butterflies does it lure?
Record what still grows beneath it

blurb: A multicoloured garden shrub that has overrun forests on three continents.
deeper: Butterflies love it, but it carpets forest floors and its leaves poison grazing animals.

links.hint: Log exactly which water body it has reached

blurb: A beautiful floating plant that can double its mat in two weeks.
deeper: Mats block light and oxygen, suffocating the water beneath. Mapping new outbreaks early is the cheapest control there is.

phenotypes.name: Autumn colour
phenotypes.hint: Leaves turned bronze or russet

phenotypes.name: Mast year
phenotypes.hint: A bumper acorn crop

links.hint: Find a fungus on or beneath it
Which birds feed in its canopy?
Who buries its acorns?

blurb: A long-lived giant that is less a tree than a town.
deeper: A mature oak supports over two thousand species, hundreds found nowhere else. Veterans can pass eight hundred years.

phenotypes.name: Autumn colour
phenotypes.hint: Leaves turned bronze or russet

phenotypes.name: Mast year
phenotypes.hint: A bumper acorn crop

links.hint: Find a fungus on or beneath it
Which birds glean its caterpillars?
Who plants its acorns?

blurb: The pale-barked keystone of eastern forests.
deeper: Oaks host more caterpillar species than any other North American trees — the baby food of nearly every songbird.

phenotypes.name: Autumn colour
phenotypes.hint: Leaves turned butter-yellow

phenotypes.name: In catkin
phenotypes.hint: Spring catkins shedding pollen

links.hint: Look for a red-capped partner at its feet

blurb: A white-barked pioneer, first to colonise open ground.
deeper: Short-lived and generous: its roots partner with fly agaric, and its soft dead wood houses tits and woodpeckers.

phenotypes.name: Autumn foliage
phenotypes.hint: Crown turned scarlet

phenotypes.name: Spring flowers
phenotypes.hint: Red tassels on bare twigs

phenotypes.name: Winged seeds
phenotypes.hint: Paired red 'helicopters'

links.hint: Find an early bee at its flowers

blurb: Red in every season: buds, flowers, leaf-stalks and autumn fire.
deeper: Among the first trees to flower, feeding early bees before leaves emerge. Its autumn colour is a sunscreen for withdrawing nutrients.

links.hint: Check the bark for D-shaped exit holes

blurb: A tall, diamond-barked tree now fighting for survival.
deeper: Emerald ash borer has killed hundreds of millions of ash. Surviving 'lingering ash' are precious to breeders — map them.

links.hint: Inspect the trunk for a spotted sap-feeder
Record what it is shading out

blurb: A fast, foul-smelling tree that sprouts from pavement cracks.
deeper: It poisons neighbouring plants through its roots and is the favourite host of the spotted lanternfly.

links.hint: Who carries its seeds away?
Every fig depends on a wasp — find any insect on it

blurb: A fig that walks: aerial roots become trunks until one tree is a grove.
deeper: Each fig species has its own tiny wasp pollinator. Fruiting year-round, a banyan is a keystone feeding entire bird and bat communities.

links.hint: Which birds eat the yellow fruit?
Who visits the spring flowers?

blurb: The village pharmacy tree, with honey-scented spring flowers.
deeper: Its bitter compounds deter over two hundred insect pests, yet its flowers feed bees and its fruit feeds birds.

links.hint: Find the nectar-feeders in its bloom
It follows rivers and floodplains

blurb: The great hollow-bearing eucalypt of inland waterways.
deeper: Hollows take a century or more to form and house parrots, owls, bats and possums. An old tree cannot be replaced by planting.

phenotypes.name: Yellow-orange form
phenotypes.hint: Cap orange-yellow rather than scarlet

links.hint: Which tree is it partnered with?

blurb: The red-and-white toadstool of fairy tales. Poisonous.
deeper: The mushroom is only the fruit. Below ground its threads sheath tree roots, trading water and minerals for sugar.

links.hint: Identify the dead wood it is consuming

blurb: Thin, velvety brackets banded like a turkey's fan.
deeper: One of the great recyclers: it dismantles lignin, the toughest part of wood, returning dead trees to the soil.

links.hint: Identify its host tree

blurb: Sulphur-yellow shelves erupting from old trunks.
deeper: It hollows the heartwood of veteran trees — bad for timber, superb for the owls and bats that need hollows.

links.hint: It grows on one kind of tree only — find it

blurb: A pale, rounded hoof found only on birch.
deeper: Ötzi the Iceman carried it 5,300 years ago. Its old brackets become beetle nurseries.

links.hint: Log it in disturbed, grassy ground

blurb: A shaggy white cylinder that melts into black ink within a day.
deeper: It digests its own cap to release spores — and its threads hunt nematode worms in the soil.

links.hint: Identify the log or trunk it is fruiting from

blurb: Pale, shell-shaped tiers on dead hardwood — even in frost.
deeper: A winter-fruiting recycler that also lassoes and digests nematodes for nitrogen.

links.hint: Record which tree it is growing on

blurb: Egg-yolk crusts on twigs, walls and gravestones.
deeper: A lichen is a fungus farming algae. This one thrives on nitrogen, so its abundance maps fertiliser and traffic pollution.

phenotypes.name: White monarch (nivosus)
phenotypes.hint: Greyish-white where orange should be — very rare

links.hint: Its caterpillars eat one family of plant only — find it nearby
Find the nectar flowers fuelling the adults

blurb: The orange-and-black migrant that crosses a continent in relays.
deeper: No single butterfly completes the round trip. The autumn 'super generation' lives eight times longer than its parents to reach Mexico.

phenotypes.name: White-hindwing form
phenotypes.hint: Hindwings largely white

phenotypes.name: Dorippus form
phenotypes.hint: Lacks the black-and-white wingtips

links.hint: Find the giant milkweed its caterpillars eat
Find its nectar plants

blurb: The tawny 'African monarch', painted in Egyptian tombs 3,500 years ago.
deeper: Unpalatable thanks to its milkweed diet, it is copied by several harmless butterflies that borrow its warning colours.

links.hint: Find the thistle or nettle its caterpillars tent
Find its nectar flowers

blurb: The most widespread butterfly on Earth.
deeper: Its 12,000 km round trip between Africa and the Arctic Circle, flown over several generations, is the longest known butterfly migration.

links.hint: Its caterpillars eat a stinging plant — find the patch
Find its late-season nectar source

blurb: Velvet black with red sashes; a strong-flying migrant.
deeper: Its caterpillar lives inside a folded nettle leaf. In autumn the adults get drunk on rotting fruit and ivy nectar.

links.hint: Record what it is foraging on

blurb: The managed pollinator, dancing directions to its sisters.
deeper: A returning forager's waggle dance encodes distance and direction relative to the sun. Outside its native range it is, in effect, livestock.

links.hint: Record the flowers it works
Queens nest underground in rough, undug ground

blurb: A big, furry, early-flying bee with a buff-white tail.
deeper: It 'buzz-pollinates', shaking pollen loose at a pitch near middle C — the only way tomatoes and many wildflowers release it.

links.hint: Record the flowers it works
Queens overwinter in leaf litter — leave the leaves

blurb: The yellow-vested bumblebee of eastern gardens.
deeper: Only new queens survive winter, alone underground. Every bee you see in spring is a founding queen.

links.hint: Find the aphid-laden plant it patrols
A larger rival is moving in — find it

blurb: The classic red beetle with seven black spots.
deeper: One ladybird eats around five thousand aphids in its life. Its spiky grey larva looks nothing like the adult.

phenotypes.name: Succinea
phenotypes.hint: Orange with up to nineteen black spots

phenotypes.name: Spectabilis
phenotypes.hint: Black with four red spots

phenotypes.name: Conspicua
phenotypes.hint: Black with two red spots

links.hint: Record the native insects sharing its plant

blurb: A shape-shifting ladybird in dozens of colour forms.
deeper: Released for pest control, it now out-eats native ladybirds and preys on their larvae. Look for the 'M' behind its head.

links.hint: Its young live underwater — log it at its pond
Find the smaller insects it hunts

blurb: A big green-and-blue dragonfly that migrates like a bird.
deeper: It takes three generations to complete one annual north–south migration. The nymph is a pond's top insect predator.

links.hint: Log it at the pond where it breeds
Find the insects it catches on the wing

blurb: A large, sky-blue dragonfly that rarely stops patrolling.
deeper: It is spreading north as the climate warms — your records document that shift in real time.

links.hint: Log it over long, unlit, damp grass

blurb: The J-stroke flasher of warm dusk lawns.
deeper: Each species has its own flash code. Larvae live two years in damp leaf litter — raked, lit-up gardens have none.

links.hint: Log it in the rough ground it sings from

blurb: The glossy black fiddler of warm evenings.
deeper: Chirp rate rises with temperature — count chirps in a fixed interval and you have a thermometer.

links.hint: Find the tree it is singing from

acoustic.sounds: A rising, whining buzz like a tiny circular saw

blurb: The buzz-saw soundtrack of high summer.
deeper: Nymphs spend years underground sipping root sap. Look for their split, empty shells clinging to bark.

links.hint: Identify and log the ash tree it is attacking

blurb: A metallic-green beetle and the costliest forest insect in North American history.
deeper: Larvae carve S-shaped galleries under bark, girdling the tree. Never move firewood — that is how it travels.

links.hint: Find its favourite host tree nearby

blurb: A spotted grey planthopper with startling red hindwings.
deeper: It lays putty-like egg masses on anything — cars, stone, pallets. Reports of egg masses in new areas matter most.

links.hint: Record what flies into its web

blurb: The cross-backed orb weaver of autumn hedges.
deeper: It eats and re-spins its web most nights, recycling the silk protein.

links.hint: Whose fallen leaves is it pulling under?
Find a bird hunting it

blurb: The deep-burrowing nightcrawler that drags leaves underground.
deeper: Darwin spent forty years on it. A gardener's friend in Europe — but in once-glaciated North American forests it strips the leaf litter wildflowers need.

links.hint: Log the permanent pond it needs
It eats anything it can swallow — what lives alongside it?

blurb: A dinner-plate frog with a foghorn voice.
deeper: Farmed worldwide for its legs, escapees now eat native frogs and spread a lethal amphibian fungus.

links.hint: Log the temporary pool it breeds in
Outside spring it lives in woodland — record the trees

acoustic.sounds: A piercing, rising peep, repeated — sleigh-bells en masse

blurb: A thumbnail-sized frog whose chorus is the sound of spring.
deeper: It survives winter partly frozen, its cells protected by glucose antifreeze, and sings from pools too short-lived for fish.

links.hint: Log the pond where it spawns
It hunts slugs and insects on damp nights

acoustic.sounds: A low, purring croak, like a distant motorbike

blurb: The smooth-skinned garden frog with a dark eye-mask.
deeper: A garden pond without fish is among the most valuable things one household can give wildlife.

links.hint: Record the insects it gathers to eat
Log the rain pool where it breeds

blurb: A warty, black-crested toad under every monsoon streetlight.
deeper: It gathers under lamps to eat the insects they attract. Introduced to Madagascar, it now threatens predators with no defence against its toxins.

links.hint: Log the water body it is breeding in

acoustic.sounds: A low, purring trill like a distant idling engine

blurb: A huge toad released to save sugar cane — which it did not.
deeper: Its toxin kills the quolls, snakes and goannas that try to eat it. Records at the invasion front guide control.

links.hint: Log the fishless vernal pool
It spends the year under woodland logs — record the trees

blurb: A stout black salamander with yellow polka dots, seen on one rainy night a year.
deeper: Its embryos host algae inside their own cells — the only known vertebrate to do so. Breeding pools are few and easily destroyed.

phenotypes.name: Melanistic
phenotypes.hint: Entirely black

phenotypes.name: Red-sided
phenotypes.hint: Red bars between the stripes

links.hint: Record the worms or frogs it hunts
Log the damp, grassy ground it needs

blurb: A striped, harmless snake of gardens and pond edges.
deeper: It can eat toxic newts and toads that would kill other predators, and overwinters in communal dens of hundreds.

phenotypes.name: Breeding colours
phenotypes.hint: Head and throat flushed bright red

links.hint: Record the insects it ambushes
Find the shrub or trunk it displays from

blurb: A crested hedge lizard — the 'bloodsucker' that sucks no blood.
deeper: Breeding males flush crimson on the head and throat within minutes, then fade again.

links.hint: Record the moths and flies it hunts at the light

blurb: The chirping wall-walker beside every porch light.
deeper: Its toes grip with millions of microscopic hairs, no glue required. It has ridden ships to nearly every warm port.

phenotypes.name: Black morph
phenotypes.hint: Jet-black coat, commoner in northern cities

phenotypes.name: White morph
phenotypes.hint: Leucistic or albino — a local celebrity

links.hint: Find the tree whose seeds it plants
What watches it from above?

blurb: The acrobatic nut-burier of city parks.
deeper: It forgets a share of its buried acorns — and so plants forests. In Britain and Italy it is displacing the native red squirrel.

links.hint: Identify the trees it depends on
Is its rival present here?

blurb: The tuft-eared native squirrel of Eurasian woods.
deeper: It survives where conifers or pine martens give it an edge over the introduced grey. Each record helps map its retreat — or return.

links.hint: Find the fruiting tree it raids

blurb: A chirruping, striped squirrel of gardens and temple walls.
deeper: A busy pollinator and seed-carrier of garden trees; its bird-like alarm call warns the whole neighbourhood.

links.hint: Record the beetles and worms it forages
Log the connected, untidy garden it needs

blurb: A snuffling night gardener in sharp decline.
deeper: One hedgehog roams a mile a night. A 13 cm gap under a fence links gardens into the territory it needs.

links.hint: Record its prey — rodents, rabbits, even worms
Log the cover where it dens

acoustic.sounds: A hoarse triple bark, or a blood-curdling winter scream

blurb: The most widespread wild carnivore on Earth.
deeper: It thrives in cities on rodents, worms and fallen fruit. In Australia, introduced foxes have driven small marsupials extinct.

links.hint: Record the insects that are flying where it hunts
It follows tree lines to water — log the route

blurb: A thumb-sized bat flickering round treetops at dusk.
deeper: It eats up to three thousand midges a night. Its calls are far above human hearing, so log it by sight at dusk.

links.hint: Record the insects flying where it hunts
It needs old trees and open water

blurb: A sturdy, glossy bat of barns, attics and streetlights.
deeper: A colony eats enough beetles each summer to spare farmers millions of crop-pest larvae. Its calls are ultrasonic — log it by sight.

links.hint: Find the fruiting trees it visits by night
Record the kind of tree the camp hangs in

acoustic.sounds: Squabbling shrieks and chatter from the roost

blurb: A fox-faced fruit bat with a wingspan over a metre.
deeper: Roost trees are used for generations and carry seeds for tens of kilometres each night. Camps are easily disturbed, so their locations are obscured.

phenotypes.name: Piebald
phenotypes.hint: Blotched white and brown

phenotypes.name: In velvet
phenotypes.hint: Summer antlers sheathed in fuzzy skin

links.hint: Record the wildflowers and saplings it browses
Log it at the woodland edge

blurb: A flag-tailed browser, most often known by its tracks.
deeper: With wolves gone, dense deer herds eat forests bare of seedlings and wildflowers — a browse line at head height is their signature.
